_note: Advanced lesson authored from COSC 220 / Runestone-style topic structure. Original prose and examples only.
title: Stacks
summary: A **stack** is a linear structure where the newest item is always handled first.
refresher: A **stack** follows **LIFO**: last in, first out. Use **push** to add to the top, **pop** to remove the top, and **peek** to read the top without removing it.
refresher_code:
push A, push B, push C
pop -> C

advanced-stack-lifo.title: LIFO means newest first
advanced-stack-lifo.body: A **stack** removes the last item that was added.
advanced-stack-lifo.example: push A, push B, push C, pop -> C
advanced-stack-lifo.notice: Only the top item is removed.
advanced-stack-lifo.mistake: If you remove A first, you are thinking like a **queue**, not a **stack**.

advanced-stack-parentheses.title: Stacks fit nested work
advanced-stack-parentheses.body: Opening symbols wait on the **stack**. A closing symbol must match the newest opening symbol.
advanced-stack-parentheses.example: ([ ]) closes the bracket before the parenthesis.
advanced-stack-parentheses.notice: Nested work finishes in reverse order.
advanced-stack-parentheses.mistake: Matching against the oldest opening symbol breaks nested expressions.

advanced-stack-trace.title: Trace the top
advanced-stack-trace.body: When tracing a **stack**, update which item is on top after every push or pop.
advanced-stack-trace.notice: The top changes after every operation.
advanced-stack-trace.mistake: Do not read from the bottom unless the prompt says to inspect the whole **stack**.

advanced-stack-parsons.title: Reverse with a stack
advanced-stack-parsons.body: Push each item, then pop until empty. The pop order is reversed.
advanced-stack-parsons.example: A, B, C becomes C, B, A
advanced-stack-parsons.notice: The second **loop** removes the newest remaining item each time.
advanced-stack-parsons.mistake: Popping too early only reverses part of the **input**.

sections.title: What is a stack?
sections.summary: A **stack** is **LIFO**: last in, first out.

blocks.body: A **stack** is a linear **data structure**. Linear means the items sit in a sequence. Stack order has one rule to remember: the newest item is on top, so it is the first item removed.

blocks.title: Watch LIFO in action
blocks.caption: Step through push, peek, and pop so the top of the **stack** is visible.

state.note: A stack removes from the same end where it adds.

steps.title: Push B
steps.body: B is newer, so B becomes the top.

steps.title: Peek
steps.body: Peek reads B without removing it.

steps.title: Pop
steps.body: Pop removes the newest item, so B comes out first.

blocks.body: That rule is called **LIFO**, which stands for last in, first out. Think about a pile of plates. You place a clean plate on top. If you need a plate later, the top plate is the easiest one to take.

blocks.title: Stack vocabulary
items: `top` is the end where pushes and pops happen.
`bottom` is the oldest item in the **stack**.
`push` adds a new item to the top.
`pop` removes and returns the top item.
`peek` or `top` looks at the top item without removing it.
`is_empty` checks whether there is anything to pop.

blocks.caption: Trace the **LIFO** rule by hand before writing code.

python.code:
stack = []
stack.append("A")
stack.append("B")
stack.append("C")
print(stack.pop())
print(stack.pop())

blocks.prompt: A **stack** receives A, then B, then C. What is popped first?
blocks.why: C was added last, so C is on top.

sections.title: The Stack ADT
sections.summary: An **ADT** names the behavior before the code details.

blocks.body: **ADT** means abstract **data type**. Abstract means you name the behavior before the implementation. For a **stack**, the behavior is add to the top, remove from the top, look at the top, and check whether it is empty.

blocks.title: Stack operations
items: `push(item)`: put item on top.
`pop()`: remove and **return** the top item.
`peek()`: **return** the top item without removing it.
`is_empty()`: **return** true if the **stack** has no items.
`size()`: **return** how many items are stored.

blocks.caption: Pop changes the **stack**. Peek does not.
blocks.wrong:
top = stack.pop()
# top item is gone now
blocks.right:
top = stack.peek()
# top item is still there
blocks.body: If the next operation still needs the top item, use peek instead of pop.

blocks.title: Empty stack rule
blocks.body: A **stack** needs a rule for empty `pop` and empty `peek`. Beginner code can **return** `None` or `null`. Some real libraries throw an error. Either way, do not ignore the empty case.

blocks.prompt: Which operation reads the top item without removing it?

sections.title: Implement a stack
sections.summary: A **stack** can be built with a **list**, dynamic **array**, deque, or linked nodes.

blocks.body: The simplest **stack** uses a **list** or dynamic **array**. Treat the end as the **top**. Adding and removing at the end is fast in the common built-in structures.

blocks.caption: A small **stack** **class** makes the operations clear.

blocks.title: Read the Python class line by line
items: `__init__` creates the empty storage **list**.
`self.items` belongs to this **stack** **object**.
`append(item)` adds to the end. We treat that end as the top.
`pop()` removes and returns the last item.
`items[-1]` means the last item in the **list**.
`len(self.items)` gives the number of stored items.

blocks.title: Implementation choice
blocks.body: **Array**/**list** stacks are simple and fast for most learning problems. Linked-list stacks are useful when you are practicing nodes and pointers, but the stack behavior stays the same.
Tracing a **stack** is quick if you draw the top. After every push, the new item becomes the top. After every pop, the next item below becomes the top.

blocks.title: Trace
items: start: []
push 4 -> [4]
peek -> 9, **stack** stays [4, 9]
pop -> 9, **stack** becomes [4]

blocks.prompt: After push 4, push 9, pop, push 2, what is on top?
blocks.why: The pop removes 9. Then 2 is pushed, so 2 is on top.

sections.title: Where stacks show up
sections.summary: **Stacks** are used when work finishes in reverse order.

blocks.title: Common stack uses
items: Undo history: the newest action is undone first.
**Function** calls: the current function finishes before the function that called it continues.
Balanced symbols: the newest opening symbol must close first.
Reversing data: pushing then popping reverses the order.
Postfix expression evaluation: numbers wait until an **operator** uses them.

blocks.caption: Balanced parentheses uses a **stack** of openings.

blocks.title: Two failure cases
blocks.body: A closing parenthesis can appear with no opening waiting. Or openings can be left on the **stack** at the end. Both mean the symbols are not balanced.

blocks.title: Match parentheses with a stack
blocks.caption: Watch opening symbols wait on the **stack** until the matching closing symbol appears.

steps.title: Read (
steps.body: An opening parenthesis waits for a future closing parenthesis.
steps.what_changed: The **stack** now remembers the newest unfinished symbol.

steps.title: Read [
steps.body: The bracket is inside the parenthesis, so it goes on top.
steps.what_changed: The bracket must close before the parenthesis can close.

steps.title: Read ]
steps.body: The closing bracket matches the top opening bracket, so pop it.
steps.what_changed: The bracket pair is finished. The parenthesis is back on top.

steps.title: Read )
steps.body: The closing parenthesis matches the remaining top item.
steps.what_changed: The **stack** is empty, so every opening symbol was closed in the right order.
